Why can radio waves go though some solids, but not all solids?

The simplest way to explain this is it has to do with the wavelength of the radio wave, and the size and structure of atoms and molecules in solid. The radio wave will only interact with (reflect off of or be absorbed by) the solid if the size of the atoms in the solid is comparable with the wavelength of the radio wave. It also has to do with the distance the wave must travel through the material. Radio waves are large (100 inches - 10 meters) so they tend to pass easily though thin layers of common home building materials (like wood and brick). However, in a large skyscraper made predominantly of thick metal like iron, it would be significantly harder for a Radio wave to pass through the walls of the building. It is analogous to how light can pass through glass but not through a brick wall.

Radio waves travel forever essentially. They emanate from their source as a spherical wave. The real question is how far away can you still detect the signal. For instance, you would need a very high quality radio wave detector to detect a radio wave coming from Earth if you were standing on Mars..but you would still in theory be able to detect the signal. So radio waves can travel from Kanas to anywhere they please it's just a matter of how strong your antenna is.
